Gastrointestinal Disorders

Acute Abdominal Pain

Acute abdominal pain is a risk-management diagnosis problem. The ED task is to identify instability, surgical abdomen, vascular catastrophe, pregnancy emergencies, and high-risk patients while still treating pain and nausea.

Board trap: A normal WBC, mild pain, or negative early CT does not end the case when the patient is elderly, pregnant, immunocompromised, postoperative, or worsening.

ACUTE ABDOMINAL PAIN

INTRODUCTION AND EPIDEMIOLOGY

Abdominal pain is common and the differential shifts with age, sex, pregnancy status, surgery history, geography, medications, immune status, and time from onset. Serious disease can begin with nonspecific symptoms, and extra-abdominal disease such as MI, pneumonia, DKA, toxicologic syndromes, and testicular pathology can present as abdominal pain.

Think in parallel: resuscitate unstable patients, treat symptoms, and keep the differential open until serial exam and targeted testing narrow the problem.

PATHOPHYSIOLOGY

VISCERAL PAIN

Visceral pain is vague and poorly localized because afferent fibers enter the spinal cord bilaterally. Foregut pain tends to be epigastric, midgut pain periumbilical, and hindgut pain suprapubic. Migration from visceral to parietal pain is a classic warning that inflammation is localizing.

Tintinalli source

Table 71-1

Visceral pain features by embryologic origin.

PARIETAL PAIN

Parietal pain comes from irritation of the parietal peritoneum and is sharper, more localized, and worsened by movement, cough, heel strike, or palpation. Guarding, rigidity, rebound, and pain with coughing increase concern for peritonitis, though high-risk patients may lack classic findings.

REFERRED PAIN

Referred pain maps embryology and shared innervation: diaphragmatic irritation may refer to shoulder, biliary disease to right scapula, splenic pathology to left shoulder, and ureteral pain to groin or testicle. Rosen's referred-pain and colic figures add pattern recognition to Tintinalli's visceral pain table.

CLINICAL FEATURES

CLINICAL RISK

High-risk abdominal pain includes shock, peritonitis, severe pain out of proportion, syncope, fever, immunocompromise, pregnancy, advanced age, cognitive impairment, inability to communicate, prior abdominal surgery, vascular disease, malignancy, transplant, and steroid or immunomodulator use. The diagnosis is often delayed because early symptoms and labs can look deceptively mild.

HISTORY AND PHYSICAL EXAMINATION

Use OPQRST plus associated symptoms, prior episodes, diagnostics, treatments, surgeries, menstrual and pregnancy history, medications, alcohol/drug exposure, travel, food, living situation, and immune status. Examine the whole patient: vitals, skin, cardiopulmonary exam, abdomen, hernias, genital/testicular/pelvic/rectal exam when indicated, and serial reassessment.

Location helps but is imperfect. Tintinalli and Rosen both use location frameworks, but both warn that patient age, pregnancy, and atypical presentations distort classic patterns.

SYMPTOM TREATMENT AND FURTHER CLINICAL DIAGNOSIS

Pain

Provide analgesia and antiemetics while continuing evaluation. Opioids do not meaningfully increase diagnostic error when used carefully, and withholding analgesia is poor care. Avoid masking peritonitis with NSAIDs alone when intra-abdominal inflammation is suspected. Symptom relief is not diagnostic cure; reassess after treatment.

LABORATORY TESTING

Labs refine the differential but do not replace history and physical examination. Use pregnancy testing, CBC, electrolytes, renal function, LFTs, lipase, lactate, urinalysis, coagulation studies, STI testing, ECG, troponin, and other tests only when they answer a clinical question. A single normal WBC cannot exclude appendicitis, ischemia, perforation, or serious elderly disease.

DIAGNOSTIC IMAGING

Plain Radiographs

Plain films have limited sensitivity but can help identify free air, obstruction patterns, some foreign bodies, or chest processes masquerading as abdominal pain. If peritonitis or shock suggests surgery, do not delay consultation for low-yield films.

Ultrasound

Ultrasound is preferred for biliary disease, pregnancy-related questions, selected gynecologic disease, AAA screening, hydronephrosis, and bladder volume. Operator skill and body habitus limit accuracy.

POCUS

POCUS can rapidly assess free intraperitoneal fluid, aorta, gallbladder, kidneys, bladder, and selected pelvic questions. It is a decision accelerator, not a final answer for all abdominal pain.

Abdominal-Pelvic CT Scanning

CT is sensitive for many adult abdominal emergencies and is often the test of choice for appendicitis, diverticulitis, obstruction, perforation, abscess, malignancy, and uncertain diagnosis. CT choice, contrast strategy, and timing should follow the clinical question and local protocol.

TREATMENT

Treatment includes resuscitation, analgesia, antiemetics, fluids, correction of derangements, source control, consultation, and disease-specific care. Patients with peritonitis, shock, ischemia, perforation, obstruction with toxicity, ruptured ectopic pregnancy, ruptured AAA, or unstable GI bleeding require immediate escalation.

ANTIBIOTICS

Give empiric antibiotics when intra-abdominal infection or sepsis is suspected. Cover enteric gram-negative and anaerobic organisms, and broaden for high-risk community-acquired or healthcare-associated infection. Antibiotics do not replace source control; they buy time for definitive management.

Tintinalli source

Table 71-5

Antibiotic regimens for intra-abdominal infections.

DISPOSITION AND FOLLOW-UP

Surgical or specialty consultation is required once a surgical diagnosis is made or strongly suspected. Discharge is reasonable only when symptoms improve, serious disease is unlikely, follow-up is reliable, oral intake is adequate, and return precautions are explicit. Patients with unclear diagnosis must understand the uncertainty and timing for reassessment.

SPECIAL POPULATIONS

WOMEN

Women with lower abdominal or pelvic pain require pregnancy status assessment, gynecologic differential, STI/PID consideration, and pelvic ultrasound when indicated. Ectopic pregnancy, ovarian torsion, ruptured ovarian cyst, tubo-ovarian abscess, and PID cannot be safely dismissed by a benign early abdominal exam.

Tintinalli source

Table 71-6

Common gynecologic causes of lower abdominal/pelvic pain.

ELDERLY PATIENTS

Elderly patients often have vague symptoms, muted fever, minimal leukocytosis, and high mortality when diagnosis is delayed. Cholecystitis, bowel obstruction, mesenteric ischemia, AAA, diverticulitis, perforation, and malignancy are common dangerous causes. Any acute abdominal pain in an elderly patient deserves a low threshold for observation, imaging, and recheck.

BARIATRIC SURGERY PATIENTS

Bariatric anatomy changes symptom patterns and creates risks of leak, internal hernia, obstruction, volvulus, marginal ulcer, dumping, bleeding, and nutritional/metabolic complications. A normal early exam does not exclude internal hernia or leak.

Tintinalli source

EPIPLOIC APPENDAGITIS

Epiploic appendagitis causes localized pain, often LLQ, and may mimic diverticulitis or appendicitis. Patients are usually not systemically ill. Treatment is supportive pain control; antibiotics are not indicated and most cases resolve in 1 to 2 weeks.

THE POSTOPERATIVE PATIENT WITH ACUTE ABDOMINAL PAIN

ILEUS AND EARLY POSTOPERATIVE BOWEL OBSTRUCTION

Postoperative pain requires attention to timing, surgery type, fever, tachycardia, peritonitis, distention, vomiting, wound findings, drainage, and ability to pass stool or flatus. Ileus is common early, but mechanical obstruction, leak, abscess, hemorrhage, urinary retention, and abdominal compartment syndrome are dangerous mimics. Escalate when pain worsens, vitals deteriorate, oral intake fails, or exam evolves.
